seo.title: Learning & Leadership Program
seo.description: Ocean education, youth programs, and capacity building for conservation leaders.

hero.title: Strengthen Coastal Education
hero.text2: Lasting conservation depends on knowledge, skills and local leadership. Using the ocean as a classroom, this programme helps youth, community members and practitioners build the confidence and experience to lead change. It is delivered together with the KCW-CBO, the Kuruwitu BMU, schools and local practitioners, with OA as facilitator and programme partner. Learning and lessons-sharing are cross-cutting and intergenerational, not youth-only.

whatWeDo.heading: What We Do
whatWeDo.text: Youth for Oceans (Y4O) bringing 10,000+ students to the living classroom at Kuruwitu across 50 schools.
whatWeDo.text2: 300+ international students, 40+ interns, and 15 filmmakers trained to advocate for coastal fisheries globally.
whatWeDo.text3: Leadership development and citizen science building community capacity for long-term stewardship.
whatWeDo.text4: Kuruwitu isn't just a marine sanctuary - it's a living classroom where conservation becomes real. Every year, students from across Kilifi County arrive to snorkel above coral gardens, identify reef species, and hear stories from community divers about what the reef looked like before, and what it looks like now. This is ocean literacy rooted in living evidence, not textbook theory.
whatWeDo.text5: Since 2016, Oceans Alive has walked alongside coastal communities to turn their vision for a healthy ocean into reality. We don't just teach - we build learning platforms where knowledge flows in every direction: from elders to youth, from fishers to scientists, from Kuruwitu to the world.
whatWeDo.text6: Education here is cross-cutting and intergenerational. When primary school children plant corals alongside certified community divers, when international students learn permaculture from Mama Karanga women, when African Leadership University students document fisher stories through Project REEL - that's when conservation becomes a movement, not a project.
whatWeDo.text7: Building Ocean Ambassadors from Kilifi to the World
whatWeDo.text8: Over 10,000 school children have stepped into the ocean at Kuruwitu. Not as tourists, but as learners. They've planted corals with community divers, documented marine species, learned permaculture from LIFT Network women, and carried those lessons home.
whatWeDo.text9: Seven schools now partner directly with the Y4O program for long-term coral management and restoration education. International students - 300 from Europe and North America, 13 from African Leadership University - arrive to learn, then leave as ambassadors lobbying for sustainable coastal fisheries management globally. Fifteen filmmakers have been trained to tell these stories. Ten films have reached screens worldwide.
whatWeDo.text13: Intergenerational knowledge doesn't live in reports - it lives in stories. Project REEL trains young filmmakers to document fisher voices, community wisdom, and the Kuruwitu journey. These aren't promotional videos; they're living archives of what works, what failed, and why it matters.
whatWeDo.text18: What began at Kuruwitu is now recognized on world stages. The Fisher Folk Academy represents a model that centers community leadership, not external consultants. From IUCN conferences in Marseille, Monaco, and the Asia-Pacific region to the 2022 Blue Champions Award, the world is watching - and learning.
whatWeDo.text24: Community members, students and visitors contribute to monitoring and research through toolkits, templates and educational materials, supporting conservation across the Kilifi County BMU network.
